newsitem.title: USA: FBI reports three percent drop in serious crime.
newsitem.headline: FBI reports three percent drop in serious crime.

text.p: Serious crime decreased by three percent in the United States in the first six months of 1996, and such crimes dropped the most in the biggest U.S. cities, the FBI reported on Saturday.

Cities with populations over 1 million -- including New York, Chicago and Los Angeles -- recorded the greatest decline in the kinds of violent crimes and crimes against property that make up the FBI's serious crime statistic.
President Clinton hailed the statistics and said they showed that serious crime had declined for the fifth year in a row, the longest period of decline in a quarter century.

The FBI's statistics are based on a crime index of selected violent and property offences. The agency supplied data for individual cities, but no aggregate figures for the number of serious crimes committed.
Mid-sized cities, with populations from 500,000 to 999,999, saw no change in the first half of 1996, but other cities showed a drop in serious crime, the FBI said in a statement.

Law enforcement agencies reported 196,031 serious crimes in New York in the first six months of 1996, down from 219,130 in the same 1995 period, according to the statistics. The number of murders fell to 507 from 574.

In Washington, which had in recent years earned the nickname of "Murder Capital", the number of serious crimes reported fell to 32,937 from 32,977, although the number of murders actually rose to 199 from 158.
There were also decreases in serious crimes in suburban and rural areas.
Clinton cited his administration's efforts to put more police officers on the streets and take guns out of criminals' hands.

"We are making a difference. Today, our neighbourhoods are safer, and we are restoring the American people's confidence that crime can be reduced," Clinton said in a statement released by the White House.
"But our work is not done. We must continue to move in the right direction by adding more police officers, cracking down on gangs, and reducing gun and drug violence," he said.

The FBI's statistics were in line with reports from New York City, which just completed its safest year in three decades, with a steep drop in the number of random killings and declines in such serious crimes as rape, robbery and assault.
